extracted.intended_audience: general readers and writers of essays/creative nonfiction interested in nature, manners, society, and moral reflection
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and aesthetic principles for composing moral and nature essays and for portraying manners, gifts, and social life with authenticity and feeling. Emphasizes sincerity, original behavior, and truthful depiction over artifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue should be 'warm with life', not merely in costume or smartly epigrammatic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'strut and bridle' and speeches that are only in costume; Scott's dialogue, though clever, 'does not please on the second reading: it is not warm with life.' By contrast, Shakespeare's speakers 'do not strut and bridle' — aim for speech that is naturally great and alive rather than theatrical or merely witty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original manners and behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Portray manners that are original and commanding rather than learned conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True high behavior should appear native to the character, not something 'learned' at court; the best examples are those whose manners 'were never learned there, but were original and commanding,' giving protection and stature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtesy as an inward quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Courtesy in character should be a natural emanation of genius or nature — 'not courteous, but courtesy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elegance 'comes of no breeding, but of birth.' In fiction and portraiture, show courtesy as an intrinsic quality of the person (a moral radiance), not as mere outward ceremony or breeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid superficial social portraiture (fashion vs. true honor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Depict fashion and high society as often superficial; true worth is found in the 'heart of love' rather than painted courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fashion's valued advantages 'thrive in very confined localities' and lose value outside them; show how social extravagance is relative and often shadowy — the worth of things must vindicate taste, and love/heart is the true creator of honor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gift as a portion of the giver
rubrics_metrics.description: The true gift should be a portion of thyself; gifts should represent the giver's life, talent, or biography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer gifts that express the giver's nature — 'the poet brings his poem; the shepherd, his lamb; the painter, his picture.' Treat purchased jewelry and symbolic tokens as 'apologies for gifts' rather than true offerings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate choice of gifts (flowers, fruits, necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose gifts that are fit to the occasion: flowers and fruits are always suitable; necessity gifts are also appropriate when demanded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flowers assert beauty beyond utility; fruits admit imaginative value and are proportionate to labor; when genuine need exists, provide necessities — letting the petitioner judge his own necessity is heroic and fitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receiving gifts with dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: One should receive gifts well, avoiding unbecoming excess of either joy or sorrow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receiving can feel like degradation if independence is invaded; the well-bred receiver neither flaunts delight nor shame. Emerson invokes the Buddhist maxim 'Do not flatter your benefactors' and praises modest, equal reciprocation rather than indebtedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid euphuism and frivolity in nature writing
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing about nature, avoid ornate, affected style ('euphuism') and frivolous treatment of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'dilettantism in nature is barren and unworthy' — the 'fop of fields' is no better than his city counterpart. Treat nature with sincerity and reserve, not superficial prettiness or fashionable ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey nature's restorative and moral power
rubrics_metrics.description: Present natural scenes as medicinal, sobering, and morally ennobling — nature can shame false religion and false heroics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use images like 'the tempered light of the woods' and 'Indian summer' to show nature's capacity to heal and enlarge the soul; emphasize how immersion in nature strips away 'the knapsack of custom' and reveals deeper realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find enchantment in ordinary places
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on exotic locales; the meeting of sky and earth and the essentials of beauty can be found even on the humblest hillock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overpraising particular grand scenery; the 'point of astonishment is the meeting of the sky and the earth,' available everywhere. Encourage writers to perceive universal beauty rather than seeking only famous sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance human presence with nature's beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: A landscape's beauty often feels incomplete or 'unreal' until matched by human figures of genuine moral quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson suggests that 'the beauty of nature must always seem unreal and mocking, until the landscape has human figures that are as good as itself.' In narrative or descriptive work, consider how human character complements or contrasts with natural grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use motion and rest as foundational themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize 'Motion or change and identity or rest' as primary dualities of nature and a structural theme for thought and depiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In describing natural processes or composing thematic work, attend to the interplay of change and permanence (motion and rest) as organizing principles that explain formation and transformation across scales.
